t: The Modern AI Stack: A Map

b.t: Building AI products means picking tools across several layers. Knowing the layers helps you choose and combine frameworks instead of comparing apples with oranges.

r: Hugging Face Transformers, Datasets, PEFT, TRL
vLLM, SGLang, TGI, llama.cpp, Ollama, TensorRT-LLM
OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini APIs; LiteLLM, OpenRouter
LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, Semantic Kernel, DSPy
LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, Pydantic AI, smolagents
FAISS, Chroma, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone, Elasticsearch
Instructor, Outlines, Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard
LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, RAGAS, DeepEval, promptfoo, TruLens
FastAPI, Streamlit, Gradio, Chainlit, Next.js + Vercel AI SDK

i: Frameworks live at different layers; most products combine several.
Compare tools within a layer (vLLM vs TGI), not across layers (vLLM vs LangChain).
Protocols (MCP, A2A) connect components across vendors.

t: Deep Learning Frameworks: PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX

b.t: Developed by Meta AI, now governed by the **PyTorch Foundation** (Linux Foundation). Dominant in research and LLMs.

i: **Eager execution** (define-by-run) with dynamic graphs — feels like normal Python.
Autograd, `torch.nn` modules, `torch.compile` for graph compilation and speedups (PyTorch 2.x).
Distributed training: DDP, FSDP; ecosystem: torchvision, torchaudio, Lightning.

b.t:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(768, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 2))
x = torch.randn(4, 768)
loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(x), torch.tensor([0, 1, 1, 0]))
loss.backward()                      # autograd computes gradients
Google's framework; strong production tooling (TF Serving, TFLite / LiteRT for mobile, TF.js). **Keras 3** is multi-backend: the same Keras code runs on **TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch**.

Google's library for high-performance numerical computing: NumPy-like API plus composable transformations — `jit` (XLA compilation), `grad` (autodiff), `vmap` (vectorisation), `pmap`/sharding (parallelism). Used for large-scale training on TPUs (Gemini, Gemma research); neural-net libraries on top: Flax, Optax.

import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
f = lambda x: jnp.sum(x ** 2)
jax.grad(f)(jnp.array([1.0, 2.0]))   # Array([2., 4.])

**ONNX** (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open model format; **ONNX Runtime** runs exported models efficiently across hardware (CPU, GPU, mobile), common for deploying embedding models and classifiers.

i: PyTorch dominates LLM research and training; `torch.compile` adds speed.
Keras 3 runs on TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch backends; TF excels at mobile/production tooling.
JAX offers jit/grad/vmap on XLA; ONNX makes models portable.

b.t: Hugging Face is the hub of open AI: **models, datasets and Spaces (demos)** plus libraries.

r: thousands of pretrained models with a common API (`AutoModel`, `pipeline`)
post-training: SFTTrainer, DPOTrainer, GRPOTrainer, reward modelling
run the same training code on CPU/GPU/multi-GPU/TPU
embeddings and rerankers (now maintained by HF)
Text Generation Inference (TGI) / Text Embeddings Inference (TEI)

b.t:
from transformers import pipeline
clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
clf("I love building RAG systems!")      # [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.99...}]

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", torch_dtype="auto")
Model cards document intended use, licence, training data and limitations; `safetensors` is the safe, fast weight format (no arbitrary code execution like pickle).

i: transformers + datasets + tokenizers form the core; PEFT and TRL handle fine-tuning and alignment.
`pipeline()` gives one-line inference for common tasks.
Prefer safetensors weights and read model cards and licences.

b.t: Broadest integration ecosystem; v1 centres on `create_agent` + middleware, built on LangGraph. Covered in depth in its own topic.
Data-centric: ingestion, indexing, advanced retrieval, LlamaParse, Workflows and agents. Covered in its own topic.

Production-oriented framework built around **Pipelines** of **Components** (retrievers, embedders, generators, routers) connected explicitly as a directed graph (loops allowed). Haystack 2.x components are simple Python classes with `@component` and typed inputs/outputs; it also supports agents and serialises pipelines to YAML.

from haystack import Pipeline
from haystack.components.builders import PromptBuilder
pipe = Pipeline()
pipe.add_component("retriever", retriever)
pipe.add_component("prompt", PromptBuilder(template="Context: {% for d in documents %}{{d.content}}{% endfor %} Q: {{question}}"))
pipe.add_component("llm", generator)
pipe.connect("retriever.documents", "prompt.documents")
pipe.connect("prompt", "llm")

SDK for .NET, Python and Java that integrates LLMs into enterprise apps through **plugins** (functions the model can call), planners and memory connectors. Its agent capabilities have converged into the **Microsoft Agent Framework**.

"**Programming — not prompting — language models.**" You declare **signatures** (`"question -> answer"`) and **modules** (`dspy.Predict`, `dspy.ChainOfThought`, `dspy.ReAct`); **optimisers** (e.g. MIPROv2, BootstrapFewShot, GEPA) then automatically tune prompts and few-shot examples against a metric.

import dspy
dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-5.4-mini"))
qa = dspy.ChainOfThought("question -> answer")
qa(question="What is hybrid search?").answer

i: Haystack = explicit pipelines of typed components.
Semantic Kernel = enterprise plugins/planners, converging into Microsoft Agent Framework.
DSPy compiles declarative signatures/modules into optimised prompts using a metric.

r: crews of role-based agents, tasks; Flows
successor to AutoGen & Semantic Kernel; .NET + Python

i: **Control vs convenience** — graph/workflow frameworks (LangGraph, MAF workflows, ADK workflow agents) give precise control; high-level ones (CrewAI crews, Agents SDK) are faster to start.
**Durability & HITL** — need pause/resume over hours? Prefer frameworks with checkpointing.
**Ecosystem** — cloud (Azure → MAF, GCP → ADK, AWS → Strands), model vendor, language (.NET, TS, Java).
**Observability** — OpenTelemetry support, tracing integrations.
**Team skills & maturity** — release stability, docs, community.
Each agent framework centres on a different abstraction: graphs, crews, runners, workflow agents, code actions.
Choose by control needs, durability, ecosystem, observability and team skills.
Many teams mix frameworks via MCP and A2A.

r: PagedAttention, continuous batching, OpenAI-compatible server, broad model support
RadixAttention prefix caching, fast structured generation, strong for agents
C/C++ inference, GGUF quantization, CPU/Apple Silicon
developer-friendly local model runner built on llama.cpp

b.t: Together AI, Fireworks, Groq (LPU hardware), Cerebras, Replicate, Baseten, Modal, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Google Vertex AI — host open and proprietary models behind APIs.

i: **LiteLLM** — Python SDK + proxy that exposes 100+ providers through an **OpenAI-compatible** interface, with budgets, fallbacks, load balancing and logging.
**OpenRouter** — hosted router/marketplace for many models behind one API key.
Cloud API gateways (Portkey, Kong AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway) add caching, rate limits and observability.

b.t:
from litellm import completion
completion(model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}])
completion(model="ollama/llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}])
The OpenAI-compatible API as a lingua franca
vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, LiteLLM and many providers expose `/v1/chat/completions`, so the same client code can target different backends by changing `base_url`.

i: vLLM/SGLang/TGI/TensorRT-LLM for GPU serving; llama.cpp/Ollama/LM Studio for local.
LiteLLM and OpenRouter unify many providers behind one OpenAI-style API.
OpenAI-compatible endpoints let you swap backends by changing `base_url`.

r: JSON-schema constrained decoding (OpenAI Structured Outputs, Gemini schemas, Anthropic tool use)
Pydantic models + validation + automatic retries over many providers
constrained generation (regex, JSON schema, grammars) for open models
fast grammar-constrained decoding engines used inside servers
a DSL for typed LLM functions

b.t:
import instructor
from pydantic import BaseModel
from openai import OpenAI

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    vendor: str
    total: float

client = instructor.from_openai(OpenAI())
inv = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-5.4-mini", response_model=Invoice,
                                     messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ACME billed $1,250.50"}])

r: validators (PII, toxicity, regex, competitor mentions) on inputs/outputs
programmable rails (Colang) for dialogue flows, topics, jailbreak and fact checks
safety-classifier models for prompts and responses

b.t: Input validation → instruction hierarchy (system prompts) → retrieval/tool permission limits → output validation (schema + policy) → human approval for risky actions → monitoring.

i: Use native constrained decoding or Instructor/Outlines for reliable structured output.
Guardrails AI (validators), NeMo Guardrails (programmable rails) and Llama Guard (classifier) address safety.
Layer defences; no single guardrail is sufficient.

r: tracing, datasets, evaluators, prompt hub, deployment
RAG and agent metrics, test generation
pytest-style LLM tests, G-Eval, RAG/agent metrics
experiment tracking, LLM tracing and evaluation

i: **Offline**: fixed datasets before release (accuracy, faithfulness, tool-call accuracy, cost, latency).
**Online**: sampled production traces with LLM-as-judge, user feedback, guardrail triggers.
**Red-teaming**: adversarial prompts, jailbreaks, prompt injection.

b.t: The OpenTelemetry **GenAI semantic conventions** standardise span attributes for model calls (model name, token usage, etc.), so traces can flow to any backend — Langfuse, Phoenix, Datadog, Grafana.

i: Platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, Weave) trace and evaluate; libraries (RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens) compute metrics.
promptfoo targets CLI comparisons and red-teaming in CI.
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions make traces portable.

r: hosts, clients, servers; tools/resources/prompts; JSON-RPC over stdio or Streamable HTTP
Agent Cards, tasks, messages, artifacts; JSON-RPC over HTTP
event protocol for streaming agent state to UIs

b.t: **Prototype RAG chatbot** Python + LangChain or LlamaIndex + Chroma/pgvector + hosted LLM API + Streamlit/FastAPI + Langfuse.

**Production enterprise RAG** Ingestion (LlamaParse/Docling/Unstructured) → hybrid search (Qdrant/Weaviate/Elasticsearch) + reranker → LangGraph or LlamaIndex Workflows → FastAPI service → LiteLLM gateway → Langfuse/LangSmith tracing → RAGAS/DeepEval in CI.
**Agentic automation** LangGraph / Microsoft Agent Framework / Google ADK for orchestration, MCP servers for tools, human-in-the-loop approvals, durable checkpoints (Postgres), OpenTelemetry tracing.
**On-prem / private** vLLM or SGLang serving open-weight models (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, gpt-oss) + open embedding models (BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding) via TEI + pgvector/Milvus + self-hosted Langfuse.

i: What layer am I choosing for?
What are the latency, cost, privacy and compliance constraints?
How will I **evaluate** and **observe** it?
Can I swap components later (standard APIs, protocols)?
Is the project actively maintained with stable releases?
MCP standardises tool access; A2A standardises agent collaboration; OpenAI-style APIs standardise model access.
Assemble stacks per layer: ingestion, retrieval, orchestration, serving, gateway, observability, evaluation.
Favour standards and swappable components to keep up with a fast-moving field.
